中文原文

周氏宗祠为周瑜后裔于明万历三十四年（1606年）所建，又名"世德堂"，清乾隆八年（1743年）建门房连廊庑，清咸丰十年（1860年）被太平军烧毁，清光绪十七年（1891年）修建后进享堂。

20世纪50年代曾作为供销社仓库。这处宗祠原有前后三进，现存清光绪年间修建的后进享堂。建筑座西北朝东南，采用砖木结构，青砖小瓦硬山顶。

面阔五间17.8米，进深14米，脊高9.8米。内部用楠木柱和柏木梁，明间及次间梁架采用扁作，减柱抬梁造，四柱十三檩；稍间为八柱十一檩。

建筑的梁枋、雀替和斗栱均浮雕图案，内容包括麒麟、凤戏牡丹等吉祥纹饰和二十四孝图、文王访贤等历史典故。刀法遒劲流畅，线条明快清晰。

· · · · ·
English

The Zhou Family Ancestral Shrine was built in the 34th year of Wanli of the Ming (1606) by descendants of Zhou Yu, also known as "Shide Hall" (Hall of Inherited Virtue).

In the 8th year of Qianlong of the Qing (1743), the gatehouse with connecting corridors was built; in the 10th year of Xianfeng (1860) it was burned by Taiping forces; in the 17th year of Guangxu (1891) the rear worship hall was built.

In the 1950s it served as a supply and marketing cooperative warehouse.The shrine originally had three front-to-back courtyards; only the rear worship hall built during the Guangxu period survives.

The building faces southeast, with brick-wood structure, blue bricks, small tiles, and a gable roof.It is five bays wide (17.8m), 14m deep, with a ridge height of 9.8m.

The interior uses nanmu pillars and cypress beams; the main and secondary bays use flat-beam construction with column reduction and tai-beam (raised beam) structure, four pillars and thirteen purlins; the end bays have eight pillars and eleven purlins.

The beams, architraves, queti (spandrel brackets), and dougong all feature relief patterns, including auspicious decorations such as qilin and phoenix playing with peony, as well as historical allusions such as the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars and King Wen of Zhou visiting the worthy.

The carving is vigorous and fluid, with clear and lively lines.

苏州

Suzhou
65
处建筑

地区概述 / Regional Overview

苏州位于江苏省东南部，北滨长江，西临太湖，古称吴、姑苏和平江等，是吴文化的发源地，水土丰腴，从远古时期就成为长江流域重要的人类聚居地，后世长期保持富庶繁盛，人文气息浓厚，有"人间天堂""东方威尼斯"之誉。商朝末年，岐山周部落首领古公亶父的长子泰伯、次子仲雍为了避位让贤，千里南奔至长江南岸的梅里，在所谓的"荆蛮之地"创立"勾吴之国"。

周朝建立后，武王封其五世孙周章为诸侯，正式建立吴国，逐渐强盛，与中原各国争霸。公元前560年，吴王诸樊迁都至现苏州城址。公元前514年，吴王阖闾对旧城大加扩建，后世以此为苏州正式建城之始，距今已经超过2500年，一直保持原地，堪称中国历史最悠久的城市之一。

春秋后期和战国时期，吴地先后被越国和楚国吞并。秦代属于会稽郡，郡治设在吴县。西汉时期先后属于楚王、荆王和吴王封地，后仍属会稽郡。东汉时期在此设吴郡，三国时期归属孙吴政权统治。两晋南北朝时期变置不一，吴郡曾属扬州，后改吴州。隋代改称苏州，复改吴州、吴郡。唐代仍称苏州，先后属江南道、江南东道辖区。五代时期为吴越国统治区。

北宋时期称平江府，府城平面图有碑刻传世，其格局与今日苏州古城相似。元代在此设平江路，属江淮行省，元末起义军领袖张士诚在此建立大周政权。明代改平江路为苏州府，隶属南直隶。

清康熙六年（1667年）江苏建省，苏州城成为江苏巡抚、江苏布政使驻地，同时也是苏州府治和长洲、元和、吴县三县的县治，地位相当于省会，极为繁盛，下辖各县也都富甲四方。苏州地区的古城、古镇风貌犹存，其中姑苏区是苏州古城所在地，与常熟古城同被列为国家级历史文化名城。

此外，昆山市的周庄、锦溪、千灯，吴江区的同里、震泽、黎里，吴中区的甪直、木渎、东山，太仓市的沙溪，常熟市的沙家浜，张家港市的凤凰等12座古镇被列为中国历史文化名镇，现存古建筑数量之多、密度之大，在全国范围内都相当罕见。苏州地区是著名的水乡，占有太湖四分之三的面积。境内河网密布，古城、古镇和许多古建筑依水而建。

其中苏州古城拥有纵横交错的河道，与陆路共同形成两套交通系统，呈现出"河街相邻""人家尽枕河"的独特风貌，城内散布着大量的古代寺观、园林和民居，平江路、山塘街两个街区被列为中国十大历史文化名街，古韵浓厚，令人目不暇接。

苏州是古典园林之乡，被誉为江南园林的最高代表，旧城内的拙政园、留园、狮子林、沧浪亭、网师园、艺圃和环秀山庄等名园已经列为世界文化遗产，此外同里古镇的退思园、常熟的燕园均为园亭佳作，建筑、掇山、理水和花木配植技艺精湛，妙造自然，成为其他地区竞相模仿的范本。

苏州地区保存着较多的古代佛寺、道观和古塔，如戒幢律寺、开元寺、寒山寺、兴福寺、玄妙观和报恩寺塔、瑞光塔、虎丘塔、万佛石塔、罗汉院双塔、聚沙塔、楞伽寺塔等，反映了当地宗教文化的兴盛。

这一区域有大量的古代府邸、民居留存至今，太平天国忠王府、吴宅、潘宅和俞樾故居等，无论是深宅大院还是咫尺小庭，均表现出粉墙黛瓦、清新雅致的特点，是中国古代住宅建筑的精华。除此之外，苏州地区的古城门、会馆、文庙和古桥也都是富有地方特色的建筑，不容错过。

苏州今辖姑苏区（市政府驻地）、虎丘区、吴中区、相城区和吴江区5个区，代管常熟市、昆山市、太仓市和张家港市4个县级市，有国家级文物保护单位59处，省级文物保护单位114处，本书介绍国保建筑45处，省保建筑18处，其他建筑4处。

Suzhou is located in southeastern Jiangsu Province, bordering the Yangtze River to the north and Lake Tai to the west.Historically called Wu, Gusu, and Pingjiang, it is the birthplace of Wu culture.

With fertile land and abundant water, it has been an important human settlement in the Yangtze River basin since ancient times, maintaining long-term prosperity and rich cultural atmosphere, earning the reputations "Paradise on Earth" and "Venice of the East.

" At the end of the Shang Dynasty, Taibo and Zhongyong—eldest and second sons of Gugong Danfu, leader of the Zhou tribe at Qishan—fled south to Meili on the south bank of the Yangtze to yield the throne to their younger brother Jili, founding the "Gouwu Kingdom" in the so-called "land of Jingman.

" After the Zhou Dynasty was established, King Wu enfeoffed Zhouzhang, their fifth-generation descendant, as a feudal lord, formally establishing the State of Wu, which gradually grew powerful and contended with the Central Plains states.

In 560 BC, King Zhufan of Wu moved the capital to the present Suzhou city site.

In 514 BC, King Helü of Wu greatly expanded the old city, later regarded as the official founding of Suzhou—over 2,500 years ago, continuously occupying the same site, making it one of China's oldest cities.

In the late Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, Wu was successively annexed by Yue and Chu.In the Qin Dynasty it belonged to Kuaiji Commandery with the seat at Wu County.

In the Western Han it successively belonged to the fiefs of the King of Chu, King of Jing, and King of Wu, then remained under Kuaiji Commandery.

In the Eastern Han, Wu Commandery was established here; during the Three Kingdoms it was ruled by the Sun Wu regime.

During the Two Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties, administrative changes were frequent; Wu Commandery was once under Yangzhou, later changed to Wu Prefecture.

In the Sui Dynasty it was renamed Suzhou, then changed back to Wu Prefecture and Wu Commandery.

In the Tang it remained Suzhou, successively under Jiangnan Circuit and Jiangnan East Circuit.During the Five Dynasties it was ruled by the Wuyue Kingdom.

In the Northern Song it was called Pingjiang Prefecture, with a stone-carved map of the prefectural city surviving, its layout similar to today's Suzhou old city.

In the Yuan Dynasty, Pingjiang Route was established here under Jianghuai Province; at the end of the Yuan, rebel leader Zhang Shicheng established the Great Zhou regime here.

In the Ming, Pingjiang Route was changed to Suzhou Prefecture under Nanzhili (South Zhili).

In the 6th year of Kangxi (1667) of the Qing, Jiangsu Province was established, and Suzhou city became the seat of the Jiangsu Governor and Jiangsu Administrative Commissioner, as well as the seat of Suzhou Prefecture and the three counties of Changzhou, Yuanhe, and Wu—equivalent to a provincial capital, extremely prosperous, with all subordinate counties wealthy.

The ancient cities and towns of the Suzhou region retain their historic character.

Gusu District is the location of Suzhou's old city, listed as a national historical and cultural city together with the old city of Changshu.

Additionally, 12 ancient towns have been listed as Chinese historical and cultural towns: Zhouzhuang, Jinxi, and Qiandeng in Kunshan; Tongli, Zhenze, and Lili in Wujiang; Luzhi, Mudu, and Dongshan in Wuzhong; Shaxi in Taicang; Shajiabang in Changshu; and Fenghuang in Zhangjiagang.

The number and density of surviving ancient buildings here are rare nationwide.The Suzhou region is a famous water town, occupying three-quarters of Lake Tai.

The river network is dense; ancient cities, towns, and many buildings are built along water.

Suzhou's old city has crisscrossing waterways forming two transportation systems with land roads, presenting the unique features of "river and street adjacent" and "every family resting by the river," with numerous ancient temples, gardens, and residences scattered within.

Pingjiang Road and Shantang Street are listed among China's Top Ten Historical and Cultural Streets, with rich ancient charm.

Suzhou is the home of classical gardens, hailed as the highest representative of Jiangnan gardens.

Famous gardens in the old city—Humble Administrator's Garden, Lingering Garden, Lion Grove Garden, Surging Wave Pavilion, Master of Nets Garden, Garden of Cultivation, and Mountain Villa with Embracing Beauty—are listed as World Cultural Heritage.

Additionally, the Retreat and Reflection Garden in Tongli ancient town and Yan Garden in Changshu are both masterpieces, with exquisite architecture, rockery piling, water management, and plant arrangement, creating nature artificially and becoming models imitated elsewhere.

The Suzhou region preserves many ancient Buddhist temples, Taoist temples, and pagodas, such as Jiechuanglü Temple, Kaiyuan Temple, Hanshan Temple, Xingfu Temple, Xuanmiao Temple, and the Bao'en Temple Pagoda, Ruiguang Pagoda, Huqiu Pagoda, Ten-Thousand-Buddha Stone Pagoda, Luohan Yuan Twin Pagodas, Jusha Pagoda, and Lengjia Temple Pagoda, reflecting the flourishing of local religious culture.

This region has a large number of ancient mansions and residences surviving to this day, including the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom Loyal King's Palace, Wu Residence, Pan Residence, and Yu Yue's Former Residence—whether deep courtyard mansions or tiny courtyards, all display the features of whitewashed walls and dark tiles, fresh and elegant, representing the essence of ancient Chinese residential architecture.

In addition, the ancient city gates, guildhalls, Confucian temples, and old bridges of the Suzhou region are all distinctive local buildings not to be missed.

Suzhou currently administers 5 districts—Gusu (municipal government seat), Huqiu, Wuzhong, Xiangcheng, and Wujiang—and manages 4 county-level cities: Changshu, Kunshan, Taicang, and Zhangjiagang.

It has 59 national and 114 provincial cultural heritage protection units; this book introduces 45 national protected buildings, 18 provincial protected buildings, and 4 other buildings.

01 拙政园
Humble Administrator's Garden
明—清
级别 Level
世界文化遗产，第一批全国重点文物保护单位（1961年）
地址 Address
姑苏区东北街178号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
旺季70元，淡季50元
开放时间 Hours
7:30-17:30（17:00停止售票）
中文原文

江南园林论及规模之大、名望之高、沿革之复杂，拙政园堪居其首。明正德五年（1510年）御史王献臣告老还乡，买下当时已荒废的大弘寺造园隐居，取潘岳《闲居赋》"筑室种树……灌园鬻蔬……此亦拙者之为政也"之意，题名拙政园，开启了一代名园500年的曲折历史。

明嘉靖十二年（1533年）王献臣邀请文徵明（1470—1559）作《王氏拙政园记》《拙政园咏》，绘《拙政园三十一景图》，文、诗、图皆出自一代书画宗师之手，为后世所艳称。

可惜王献臣死后，其子一夜豪赌将拙政园输给徐氏。明末清初，钱谦益曾在园内构筑曲房，安置"秦淮八艳"之柳如是；清初园归大学士陈之遴，其妻徐灿为著名词人，著有《拙政园诗馀》，名园佳人两相得。

此后园林没收入官，康熙初年归吴三桂女婿王永宁，进行大规模改建，奠定了今日园貌。吴三桂叛清后园林又被没收，改属道台衙门，不久割裂为东、西两园。清乾隆十二年（1747年）东园归太守蒋棨，改名"复园"，嘉庆年间卖给海宁查氏，道光年间又归平湖吴氏。西园在乾隆年间归太史叶士宽，称"书园"。

清咸丰十年（1860年）太平军忠王李秀成将两园合并，作为忠王府的一部分。

太平天国失败后，西园还归叶氏，清光绪五年（1879年）又归张履谦，改建易名"补园"；东园则成为巡抚衙门花园，清同治十一年（1872年）归八旗奉直会馆，巡抚张之万加以修复，复称"拙政园"。

新中国成立后将东、西两园合并，1955年又并入东邻的"归田园居"旧址，共约60余亩，总称拙政园。归田园居为明末刑部侍郎王心一所建，王氏子孙世守三百余年，归入拙政园时已经荒废，重新改建后已非旧貌。

1961年拙政园被公布为第一批全国重点文物保护单位，1997年被联合国教科文组织列入世界文化遗产名录。

拙政园为宅第园林，其南有大片住宅，今改建为苏州园林博物馆，当年人们都是由住宅向北经腰门入园，如今则需从归田园居南侧进入，绕过新建园林，从东园东侧偏门入园，无法体会拙政园当初布局的意匠。

若按古代游序从腰门进入，迎面是一座黄石假山，从山洞穿过假山或循山路翻过假山，为园中主厅远香堂。这是一座四面厅，向南可隔小池欣赏入门假山，向北则面对园中主景，完成赏景次序的转换。远香堂北面设有临水平台，池岸平直，主人可在此宴客，隔水欣赏北面的池中三岛。

三岛水平展开，有如一幅水墨横卷，东岛点缀六角待霜亭，周围种橘树，秋日霜降橘红似火；中岛建长方形雪香云蔚亭，山间植梅树，冬季雪后梅香馥郁；西岛设六角荷风四面亭，立在水中央，炎炎暑夏荷风清凉。荷风四面亭向西经五折石桥通向柳荫路曲长廊，蜿蜒伸展于春日垂柳间。池北这四处景点完整展现了一年四季的风景，让人流连中体会时序的转换和轮回。

柳荫路曲东北是一座两层的见山楼，立于池中，为东园制高点，登楼既可纵览东园景致，又可向西北远眺虎丘风光。远香堂东侧的枇杷园是一处园中园，隐藏在堂南和堂东假山之后，饶以起伏的云墙。园内东侧的玲珑馆、听雨轩、海棠春坞通过游廊相连围成一处小院，院内种寿星竹，池边植芭蕉，可在馆中赏翠竹玲珑，于轩内听雨打芭蕉。

其中海棠春坞以粉壁为底，前置翠竹与玲珑山石，砖额呈书卷状，有如一幅册页小景，最为精致，春季海棠花开时节尤为动人。园外北侧山上有绣绮亭，可欣赏枇杷园、远香堂和北部池岛三面的景致。由海棠春坞沿小溪向北是梧竹幽居亭，位于狭长水池的东岸，在亭外南侧可向西眺望池外远处的报恩寺塔，浮屠塔影荡漾水间，两岸林木错叶交柯，为古典园林远借之佳例。远香堂西侧，绕过倚玉轩为沧浪亭水院，与枇杷园的山景形成呼应和对照。

池水向南蜿蜒深入，近处为小沧浪水阁，站在阁前北望，右前方的松风水阁挑出水面，迎面有小飞虹凌波横跨，其北香洲画舫微微前伸，锁住水口，背后荷风四面亭、见山楼交错迭出，景致层次极为丰富。由香洲向西为玉兰堂，从堂北经"别有洞天"门洞即进入西园。西园只有东园一半大小，曲折的水系将山体分为一北一南、一大一小两处，在山间水畔及平地空旷处布置建筑。

园中主厅为池南的"卅六鸳鸯馆—十八曼陀罗馆"，这是一座鸳鸯厅，但南向无景可赏，北向山池景致平平，较远香堂远为逊色。堂东假山顶顶部建宜两亭，当年园归两家时，在亭中不但可赏自家园亭，还可窥视邻园景色，古人戏称"劫景"。在山下北侧廊中可隔水观赏与谁同坐轩，背后隐现笠亭与浮翠阁，为西园最精雅之处。

池东的贴水游廊布置巧妙，不但左右曲折，而且高低起伏，随着水势俯仰有致；北部尽端接倒影楼，在楼内向南眺望，狭长溪流两侧左为蜿蜒长廊，右为山石花木，人工天然相映成趣。

拙政园虽更换过无数主人，并在清代有过几次大的改建，但其基本格局与格调仍保持明代的疏朗风格：远香堂北面的两山以土为主，叠石为辅，山上林木葱郁，野趣盎然；园中既有开阔的池面可供眺望，又不乏深邃的水景供人探幽；堂榭廊亭布置合宜，或为赏景之所，或作点景之笔，既与山水相称，又未喧宾夺主。

拙政园以其复杂的历史遭际、丰富的文化内涵和精雅的造园艺术成为名园翘楚，不负曲园主人俞樾所称——"名园拙政冠三吴"。

· · · · ·
English

Among Jiangnan gardens, the Humble Administrator's Garden (Zhuozheng Yuan) stands first in scale, fame, and complex history.

In the 5th year of Zhengde of the Ming (1510), Censor Wang Xianchen returned home after retiring from office, purchased the abandoned Dahong Temple to build a garden for seclusion, and took the name from Pan Yue's "Xianju Fu" (Rhapsody on Living in Leisure): "Building rooms and planting trees.

..watering the garden and selling vegetables...

this is also the governance of a humble man"—thus naming it Zhuozheng Yuan (Humble Administrator's Garden), beginning the tortuous 500-year history of this famous garden.

In the 12th year of Jiajing (1533), Wang Xianchen invited Wen Zhengming (1470-1559) to write the "Record of Wang's Humble Administrator's Garden" and "Humble Administrator's Garden Poems," and paint the "Thirty-One Scenes of the Humble Administrator's Garden"—prose, poetry, and paintings all from the hand of a master calligrapher and painter, admired by later generations.

Unfortunately, after Wang Xianchen's death, his son gambled away the garden to the Xu family in a single night.

In the late Ming and early Qing, Qian Qianyi once built curved chambers in the garden to house Liu Rushi, one of the "Eight Beauties of Qinhuai"; in the early Qing the garden passed to Grand Secretary Chen Zhilin, whose wife Xu Can was a famous poetess author of "Humble Administrator's Garden Poems"—a famous garden and a talented lady complementing each other.

Thereafter the garden was confiscated by the government; in the early Kangxi period it passed to Wang Yongning, son-in-law of Wu Sangui, who carried out large-scale reconstruction establishing today's appearance.

After Wu Sangui rebelled against the Qing, the garden was confiscated again, assigned to the circuit intendant's yamen, and soon split into eastern and western gardens.

In the 12th year of Qianlong (1747), the eastern garden passed to Circuit Intendant Jiang Qi, renamed "Fuyuan" (Restored Garden); in the Jiaqing period it was sold to the Zha family of Haining; in the Daoguang period it returned to the Wu family of Pinghu.

The western garden passed to Scholar Ye Shikuan in the Qianlong period, called "Shuyuan" (Study Garden).

In the 10th year of Xianfeng (1860), Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, merged the two gardens as part of the Loyal King's Palace.

After the Taiping defeat, the western garden returned to the Ye family; in the 5th year of Guangxu (1879) it passed to Zhang Lüqian, who rebuilt and renamed it "Buyuan" (Supplementary Garden); the eastern garden became the governor's yamen garden, and in the 11th year of Tongzhi (1872) passed to the Eight Banners Fengzhi Guildhall, where Governor Zhang Zhiwan restored it and revived the name "Humble Administrator's Garden.

" After the founding of New China, the eastern and western gardens were merged; in 1955 the former "Gui Tian Yuan Ju" (Return-to-Fields Garden) site to the east was also incorporated, totaling about 60 mu, all called the Humble Administrator's Garden.

Gui Tian Yuan Ju was built by Wang Xinyi, a late-Ming Vice Minister of Justice; his descendants maintained it for over 300 years.

By the time it was incorporated into the Humble Administrator's Garden it had fallen into disrepair, and after reconstruction it no longer retains its original appearance.

In 1961, the Humble Administrator's Garden was designated one of the first batch of National Key Cultural Heritage Sites; in 1997 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage List.

The Humble Administrator's Garden is a residence-garden, with a large residential area to the south, now converted into the Suzhou Garden Museum.

In olden days, visitors entered from the residence northward through a side gate; today one must enter from the south side of Gui Tian Yuan Ju, pass through the newly built garden, and enter through a side gate on the east side of the eastern garden—unable to experience the original layout's design intent.

Following the ancient visiting sequence through the side gate, one is greeted by a yellow-stone rockery.

Passing through a cave or climbing over the rockery leads to the main hall, Yuanxiang Tang (Distant Fragrance Hall).

This is a four-sided hall: to the south, one can admire the entrance rockery across a small pond; to the north, one faces the garden's main scenery, completing the transition of viewing sequence.

North of Yuanxiang Hall is a waterside platform with a straight pond bank, where the host could entertain guests and admire the three islands in the pond to the north.

The three islands spread horizontally like an ink-painting handscroll: the east island is dotted with the hexagonal Daishuang Pavilion (Waiting for Frost Pavilion), surrounded by orange trees—when frost falls in autumn, the oranges glow red; the middle island has the rectangular Xuexiang Yunwei Pavilion (Snow Fragrance and Cloud Luxuriance Pavilion), with plum trees on the mountain—after winter snow, the plum fragrance is rich; the west island has the hexagonal Hefeng Simian Pavilion (Lotus Wind on All Sides Pavilion), standing in the middle of the water, with cool lotus breezes in hot summer.

From Hefeng Simian Pavilion, a five-bend stone bridge leads west to the Liuyin Luqu (Willow Shade Winding Path) long corridor, winding among spring willows.

These four scenic spots north of the pond fully display the scenery of all four seasons, allowing visitors to experience the cycle of seasons while lingering.

Northeast of Liuyin Luqu is the two-story Jianshan Lou (Seeing Mountain Tower), standing in the pond as the highest point of the eastern garden; climbing the tower offers a panoramic view of the eastern garden and a distant view of Huqiu (Tiger Hill) to the northwest.

East of Yuanxiang Hall, the Pipa Garden (Loquat Garden) is a garden-within-a-garden, hidden behind rockeries south and east of the hall, enclosed by undulating cloud walls.

The Linglong Guan (Exquisite Hall), Tingyu Xuan (Listening to Rain Pavilion), and Haitang Chunwu (Crabapple Spring Courtyard) on the east side are connected by corridors to form a small courtyard, with longevity bamboo planted inside and banana trees by the pond—one can admire the exquisite green bamboo in the hall and listen to rain hitting banana leaves in the pavilion.

Haitang Chunwu is particularly exquisite: with a white wall as backdrop, green bamboo and exquisite rocks in front, and a brick lintel in scroll shape, it resembles an album-leaf painting, especially moving when crabapples bloom in spring.

On the hill north of the garden stands the Xiuqi Pavilion, offering views of the Pipa Garden, Yuanxiang Hall, and the northern pond islands on three sides.

Following a small stream north from Haitang Chunwu is the Wuzhu Youju Pavilion (Phoenix and Bamboo Secluded Residence), located on the east bank of a narrow pond; from the south side outside the pavilion, one can gaze west at the distant Bao'en Temple Pagoda, its reflection rippling on the water, with trees on both banks interlacing leaves and branches—a fine example of "borrowing scenery" in classical gardens.

West of Yuanxiang Hall, passing the Yiyu Xuan (Leaning on Jade Studio), is the Canglang Ting water courtyard, echoing and contrasting with the mountain scenery of the Pipa Garden.

The pond winds southward; nearby is the Xiaocanglang water pavilion.

Standing north from the pavilion, the Songfeng Shui Ge (Pine Wind Water Pavilion) juts out over the water to the right front, the Xiaofeihong (Little Flying Rainbow) bridge spans the waves ahead, and the Xiangzhou (Fragrant Islet) painted-boat hall extends slightly northward, locking the water mouth, with Hefeng Simian Pavilion and Jianshan Tower staggered behind—creating an extremely rich layered scenery.

West from Xiangzhou is the Yulan Tang (Magnolia Hall); passing through the "Bie You Dongtian" (Another World) gate from the north of the hall leads into the western garden.

The western garden is only half the size of the eastern garden, with winding water dividing the mountains into north-south and large-small pairs, with buildings arranged among mountains, watersides, and open flat areas.

The main hall is the "Thirty-Six Mandarin Duck Hall—Eighteen Datura Hall" south of the pond—a mandarin duck hall, but with no scenery to admire facing south and mediocre mountain-pond scenery facing north, far inferior to Yuanxiang Hall.

On top of the rockery east of the hall stands the Yiliang Pavilion (Suitable for Both Pavilion); when the garden belonged to two families, from this pavilion one could not only admire one's own garden pavilions but also peek at the neighboring garden's scenery—ancients jokingly called this "robbing scenery.

" In the corridor north of the mountain foot, one can view the Yushui Tongzuo Xuan (With Whom to Sit Pavilion) across the water, with the Li Pavilion and Fucui Pavilion faintly visible behind—the most elegant spot in the western garden.

The waterside corridor on the east of the pond is cleverly arranged, not only winding left and right but also rising and falling, following the water's contours; at the northern end it connects to the Daoying Lou (Inverted Reflection Tower), where looking south from inside the tower, the narrow stream has a winding long corridor on the left and rocks, trees, and flowers on the right—artificial and natural complementing each other delightfully.

Although the Humble Administrator's Garden has changed owners countless times and undergone several major reconstructions in the Qing, its basic layout and style still maintain the Ming Dynasty's open and spacious character: the two mountains north of Yuanxiang Hall are mainly earth with stacked stone as supplement, with lush trees and abundant wild charm; the garden has both open pond surfaces for gazing and deep water scenes for exploration; halls, pavilions, and corridors are appropriately arranged—either as viewing spots or as scenic accents, complementing mountains and water without overwhelming them.

With its complex historical vicissitudes, rich cultural connotations, and exquisite garden art, the Humble Administrator's Garden stands out among famous gardens, living up to the praise by Yu Yue, master of the Quyuan Garden—"The famous garden Zhuozheng crowns the Three Wu.

"

建筑要点 / Key Features
江南园林之首；明正德五年王献臣建；文徵明《王氏拙政园记》；东园（远香堂、见山楼）；西园（卅六鸳鸯馆、与谁同坐轩）；归田园居
02 太平天国忠王府
Mansion of King Zhong of Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
清
级别 Level
第一批全国重点文物保护单位（1961年）
地址 Address
姑苏区东北街204号
类型 Type
王府建筑/近代建筑
门票 Ticket
免费开放
开放时间 Hours
今属苏州博物馆，8:15-16:30
中文原文

清咸丰十年（1860年）四月，太平军忠王李秀成攻占苏州，十月合并拙政园及其南部宅第和东、西两侧的潘氏、汪氏住宅，扩建为忠王府，包括住宅、衙署和后花园三部分。

清同治二年（1863年）冬李鸿章攻克苏州，改忠王府为江苏巡抚行辕，清同治十一年（1872年）又改为八旗奉直会馆。这是中国现存最完整、规模最大的太平天国王府建筑，今需从苏州博物馆进入，看完博物馆再入府参观，由王府正门出馆。

今王府包括东、中、西三路，原为忠王府的衙署部分。中路为主路，沿轴线依次有照墙、大门、仪门、正殿、后堂和后殿，长约140米。其中正殿高大宽敞，通过穿廊与后堂相连，构成工字殿，是当年李秀成处理公务和主持军事会议的场所。工字殿北面的后殿供奉天父天兄神主，是举行礼拜之地。

东路建筑中，南部的戏台别具一格，由前厅、正厅和后厅组成，呈"目"字形，体现了忠王生活奢华排场的一面。此外忠王府的苏式彩绘也堪称一绝，后来虽遭清军涂抹，仍保存下323方原作；较精彩的是正殿东西次间脊桁上的两方《凤穿牡丹》，为清代苏式彩绘代表作。

· · · · ·
English

In the fourth month of the 10th year of Xianfeng of the Qing (1860), Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King (Zhong Wang) of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, captured Suzhou.

In October, he merged the Humble Administrator's Garden with its southern residence and the Pan and Wang family residences on the east and west sides, expanding them into the Loyal King's Mansion, including residential, administrative, and rear garden sections.

In the winter of the 2nd year of Tongzhi (1863), Li Hongzhang captured Suzhou and converted the Loyal King's Mansion into the Jiangsu Governor's temporary headquarters; in the 11th year of Tongzhi (1872) it was converted into the Eight Banners Fengzhi Guildhall.

This is the most complete and largest surviving Taiping Heavenly Kingdom prince's mansion in China.

Today one enters through the Suzhou Museum, visits the museum, then enters the mansion, exiting through the mansion's main gate.

The mansion today includes east, middle, and west roads, originally the administrative section of the Loyal King's Mansion.

The middle road is the main axis, with a screen wall, main gate, ceremonial gate, main hall, rear hall, and rear hall in sequence, about 140m long.

The main hall is tall and spacious, connected to the rear hall by a covered corridor to form a "gong" (I)-shaped hall—where Li Xiucheng handled official business and presided over military meetings.

The rear hall north of the gong-shaped hall enshrined the Heavenly Father and Heavenly Brother, used for worship services.

Among the east road buildings, the southern stage is distinctive, consisting of front hall, main hall, and rear hall in a "mu" (eye) shape, reflecting the luxurious and ostentatious aspect of the Loyal King's life.

Additionally, the Suzhou-style polychrome paintings of the Loyal King's Mansion are outstanding; although later painted over by Qing forces, 323 original works survive.

The most remarkable are the two "Phoenix Piercing Peony" paintings on the ridge purlins of the east and west secondary bays of the main hall—representative works of Qing-dynasty Suzhou-style polychrome painting.

03 狮子林
Lion Grove Garden
元
级别 Level
世界文化遗产，第六批全国重点文物保护单位（2006年）
地址 Address
姑苏区园林路23号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
旺季30元，淡季20元
开放时间 Hours
7:30-17:00（16:30停止售票）
中文原文

狮子林最初是座寺庙园林。元至正二年（1342年）佛教信徒为延请天如禅师到苏州，专门为其建造了"菩提正宗寺"，因为天如禅师出身于浙江天目山"狮子岩"，佛祖被称为"人中狮子"，而寺中景致也以奇石和竹子为主，其中最重要的一块形似狮子，所以此寺又被称作狮子林。狮子林在历史上因绘画知名。

最早是元至正二十三年（1363年）朱德润（1294—1365）应第二代住持卓峰禅师之请绘《师子林图》，明洪武六年（1373年）大画家倪瓒为第三代住持如海禅师绘《狮子林图》手卷，次年徐贲又绘《林十二景图》册页。

朱德润的画作已经佚失，后两件作品保存至今，此后杜琼、文徵明、王翚、恽南田和钱维城等著名画家都画过《狮子林图》。而狮子林能够保存至今，也与这些绘画杰作有很大关系。明代嘉靖年间狮子林被豪强占据，王世贞、文徵明等为之奔走呼吁，但还是沦落到私人手中。

明万历十七年（1589年）明性和尚恢复"狮子林圣恩寺"，园林部分作为寺后花园，从此寺、园分离。清康熙年间花园割出归张士俊，对假山有所改建；乾隆初年又归状元黄轩之父黄兴祖，更名涉园。

乾隆皇帝酷爱倪瓒书画，清乾隆十二年（1747年）倪瓒的《狮子林图》传入宫廷，乾隆对其推崇备至，除了题词盖印之外，还亲自摹写一幅。乾隆一直以为狮子林是倪瓒之园，早已不存，后得知此园在苏州，大喜过望，第二次南巡便携倪图到苏州实地寻访，并下旨重修狮子林，奠定了今日园貌基础，充分体现了乾隆皇帝的趣味。

狮子林在太平天国时期遭到破坏，1917年归富商贝仁元（建筑师贝聿铭叔祖）大加修缮，添建轩舫，增筑假山，使部分园景带有近代风格。新中国成立后贝氏后人将狮子林捐献给国家，2000年列入世界文化遗产名录。今狮子林包括祠堂、住宅和园林三部分。

从东路门厅进入，其北为祠堂正厅，由堂前檐廊折向西可达中路燕誉堂庭院，堂前花坛内树立几尊湖石、笋石，精雅可爱。向北穿过小方厅，院中立九狮峰，峥嵘峭拔，怪态横生，与前堂静态的花坛立石风格迥异，为游人接下来欣赏内园的湖石假山做好铺垫。九狮峰背后的粉墙上开四孔漏窗，分别嵌琴、棋、书、画镂雕，构思别致。以上皆为近代贝仁元添建。

穿过九狮峰西门即为园中主厅指柏轩，轩前有座古朴小巧的方池，上架小拱桥，桥南为狮子林主景——占地数亩的大假山，堪称中国古典园林假山之最。这座假山始建于元代，纯为石构，山下洞穴穿空，山上怪石林立，有蹬道穿梭于峰岭岩壑间，左绕右转，如入石林幻境。

全山共有21处洞口、9条山径、25座小桥，有人将其穿成4条路线，但极难辨认和记忆，游人在山间享受的也是迂曲惊骇之趣，沿途所立山石千奇万状，予人无尽的想象。大假山顶部中央是一片台地，建有卧云室作为一山之主。

假山向西伸展，延入西部大池之中，为清代添建，较东部假山稍为逊色。园林西部以水池为中心，池中点缀湖心亭和九曲桥，建筑、假山多绕池布置。北岸为园西主厅荷花厅，南出临水平台，可欣赏嶙峋的假山与池中的绿荷。

厅东有二层见山楼，介于东、西两山之间，可供人左顾右盼。厅西建筑较为密集，有真趣亭、石舫和暗香疏影楼等，是向南欣赏池景的理想之地。池西堆大型土山，驳砌山石，并营造出三叠瀑布，气势恢宏。山间主体建筑为问梅阁，体量与山体相称，隔池与东部大假山主景遥遥相对。池西土山延绵至南岸，贴墙以游廊连接扇子亭、文天祥碑亭和御碑亭等，循廊漫步山间，与攀岩穿穴相比，另有一种趣味。

在苏州现存园林中，狮子林的历史仅次于始建于宋代的沧浪亭，由于历时久远经过多次分合改建，园林被分为东部建筑、中部假山和西部水池三区，略有拼凑之感。但中园大假山极尽穿岩入穴、赏石立峰之能事，将人工叠山之工巧推到了极致。

这种赏石风气从唐代白居易的《太湖石记》开始兴起，延续到晚明南阳叠筑的弇山园、豫园，虽在明末清初之际被张南垣"平冈小坂"的天然风格取代，但到乾隆时期重又复兴，揭示出人们内心深处对"巴洛克风格"不绝如缕的迷恋。

· · · · ·
English

The Lion Grove Garden was originally a temple garden.

In the 2nd year of Zhizheng of the Yuan (1342), Buddhist believers, to invite Master Tianru to Suzhou, specially built the "Puti Zhengzong Temple" for him.

Because Master Tianru came from "Lion Rock" of Tianmu Mountain in Zhejiang, the Buddha is called the "Lion Among Men," and the temple's scenery featured strange rocks and bamboo—with the most important rock resembling a lion—hence the temple was also called Lion Grove.

The Lion Grove Garden is historically famous for paintings.

The earliest was in the 23rd year of Zhizheng (1363), when Zhu Derun (1294-1365), at the request of the second abbot Master Zhuofeng, painted the "Shizi Lin Tu" (Lion Grove Painting).

In the 6th year of Hongwu of the Ming (1373), the great painter Ni Zan painted a handscroll "Lion Grove Garden" for the third abbot Master Ruhai; the following year Xu Ben painted the album "Twelve Scenes of the Grove.

" Zhu Derun's painting is lost, but the latter two survive.Later famous painters including Du Qiong, Wen Zhengming, Wang Hui, Yun Nantian, and Qian Weicheng all painted "Lion Grove Garden.

" The garden's survival to this day owes much to these painted masterpieces.

During the Jiajing period of the Ming, the Lion Grove was occupied by powerful local figures; Wang Shizhen and Wen Zhengming campaigned on its behalf, but it still fell into private hands.

In the 17th year of Wanli (1589), Monk Mingxing restored the "Lion Grove Sheng'en Temple," with the garden as the temple's rear garden—henceforth temple and garden were separated.

During the Kangxi period of the Qing, the garden was separated and passed to Zhang Shijun, who modified the rockery; in the early Qianlong period it passed to Huang Xingzu, father of the zhuangyuan (top scholar) Huang Xuan, and was renamed She Garden (Wading Garden).

The Qianlong Emperor was passionately fond of Ni Zan's calligraphy and paintings; in the 12th year of Qianlong (1747), Ni Zan's "Lion Grove Garden" entered the imperial collection.

Qianlong admired it immensely, adding inscriptions and seals and even personally making a copy.

Qianlong had long believed the Lion Grove was Ni Zan's garden and no longer existed; upon learning it was in Suzhou, he was overjoyed.

On his second southern tour, he brought Ni's painting to visit the site in person and ordered the Lion Grove rebuilt—laying the foundation for today's appearance, fully reflecting the Qianlong Emperor's taste.

The Lion Grove was damaged during the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom period.In 1917 it passed to wealthy merchant Bei Renyuan (great-uncle of architect I.M.

Pei), who carried out major repairs, adding pavilions and boats and building new rockeries, giving parts of the garden a modern style.

After the founding of New China, the Bei family descendants donated the Lion Grove to the state; in 2000 it was inscribed on the World Cultural Heritage List.

Today the Lion Grove includes ancestral hall, residence, and garden sections.

Entering through the east road gate, to its north is the ancestral hall main hall; turning west from the hall's front eave corridor leads to the middle road Yanyu Tang (Hall of Eulogizing Fame) courtyard.

In front of the hall, a flower bed holds several Taihu rocks and bamboo shoots—elegant and lovely.

Passing north through the Xiaofang Hall (Small Square Hall), a Nine-Lion Peak stands in the courtyard—towering, precipitous, and grotesque, contrasting sharply with the static flower-bed rocks of the front hall, preparing visitors for the Taihu rockery of the inner garden.

Behind the Nine-Lion Peak, the white wall has four lattice windows inlaid with openwork carvings of qin (zither), qi (chess), shu (calligraphy), and hua (painting)—ingeniously conceived.

All the above were added by Bei Renyuan in modern times.Passing through the west gate of the Nine-Lion Peak is the main hall Zhibai Xuan (Pointing to Cypress Studio).

In front of the studio is a simple, small square pond with a small arched bridge; south of the bridge is the Lion Grove's main scene—a large rockery covering several mu, arguably the greatest rockery in Chinese classical gardens.

This rockery was first built in the Yuan Dynasty, purely of stone, with caves piercing through below and strange rocks standing above, with climbing paths winding through peaks, ridges, and ravines—turning left and right like entering a stone forest dreamland.

The entire mountain has 21 caves, 9 mountain paths, and 25 small bridges; some have traced 4 routes through it, but they are extremely difficult to identify and remember.

Visitors enjoy the winding and startling experience among the mountains, with the rocks along the way in myriad strange shapes, offering endless imagination.

At the center of the large rockery's top is a terrace with the Woyun Shi (Lying in Clouds) room as the mountain's master.

The rockery extends westward into the large western pond—added in the Qing Dynasty, slightly inferior to the eastern rockery.

The western part of the garden centers on a pond, dotted with a lake-center pavilion and a nine-bend bridge, with buildings and rockeries arranged around the pond.

The north bank has the western main hall Hehua Ting (Lotus Hall), with a waterside platform to the south for admiring the jagged rockery and green lotuses.

East of the hall is the two-story Jianshan Lou (Seeing Mountain Tower), between the east and west mountains, allowing visitors to look left and right.

West of the hall, buildings are denser, including Zhenqu Ting (True Delight Pavilion), Stone Boat, and Anxiang Shuying Lou (Hidden Fragrance and Sparse Shadows Tower)—ideal places for viewing the pond scenery to the south.

West of the pond, a large earth mountain is piled with stone retaining walls and a three-tier waterfall, creating a grand momentum.

The main building on the mountain is Wenmei Ge (Asking Plum Pavilion), proportionate to the mountain, facing the eastern large rockery across the pond.

The western earth mountain extends to the south bank, with a corridor along the wall connecting the Fan (Fan) Pavilion, Wen Tianxiang Stele Pavilion, and Imperial Stele Pavilion.

Strolling along the corridor through the mountains offers a different pleasure from climbing rocks and through caves.

Among Suzhou's surviving gardens, the Lion Grove's history is second only to the Surging Wave Pavilion founded in the Song Dynasty.

Due to its long history and multiple divisions, mergers, and reconstructions, the garden is divided into three areas—eastern buildings, central rockery, and western pond—with a slight sense of patchwork.

However, the central garden's large rockery exhausts the possibilities of piercing caves, admiring rocks, and erecting peaks, pushing the art of artificial rockery to the ultimate.

This rock-admiring trend began with Bai Juyi's "Record of Taihu Stones" in the Tang, continued to the late-Ming Yanshan Garden and Yu Garden built by Nanyang, and although replaced by Zhang Nanyuan's "flat ridges and small slopes" natural style in the late Ming and early Qing, it revived in the Qianlong period—revealing people's deep, unbroken fascination with the "Baroque style.

"

04 陆氏半园
Lu's Half Garden
清
级别 Level
1982年列为苏州市保
地址 Address
姑苏区白塔东路60号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
免费开放
中文原文

半园最早为清乾隆年间沈世奕所筑，原称止园；后归吴门太守周勖斋，更名朴园；清咸丰年间又归苏州道台陆解眉，始称半园。园内对联称"园虽得半，身有余闲，便觉天空海阔；事不求全，心常知足，自然气静神怡"，既谦逊又通达。西园原有住宅，今仅存园林。居中为水池，周围环以船厅、水榭、曲廊和半亭，栽植白皮松、黄杨、紫藤等花木。

园内建筑多以"半"为主旨，如东北角一座二层半的重檐楼阁，为苏州园林所仅见。

· · · · ·
English

The Half Garden was first built by Shen Shiyi during the Qianlong reign of the Qing, originally called Zhiyuan (Stopping Garden).

It later passed to Zhou Xuzhai, prefect of Wumen, who renamed it Puyuan (Simple Garden).

During the Xianfeng period it passed to Lu Jiemei, circuit intendant of Suzhou, and was first called Banyuan (Half Garden).

A couplet in the garden reads: "Though the garden is but half, with leisure to spare, one feels the sky vast and the sea broad; seeking not completeness in affairs, the heart is always content, naturally calm and joyful"—both humble and enlightened.

The western garden originally had a residence, but today only the garden survives.

A pond occupies the center, surrounded by a boat hall, waterside pavilion, winding corridor, and half-pavilions, planted with lacebark pine, boxwood, wisteria, and other flowers and trees.

The garden's buildings mostly follow the theme of "half"—for example, a two-and-a-half-story double-eave pavilion in the northeast corner, unique among Suzhou gardens.

05 尚志堂吴宅（苏州工艺美术博物馆）
Wu's Residence in Shangzhi Courtyard (Suzhou Arts & Crafts Museum)
清
级别 Level
第七批江苏省保（2011年）

中文原文

吴宅建于清乾隆年间，太平天国时期被忠王李秀成征用安置家眷。住宅包括东、中、西三路，中路最为气派，自南而北依次有门厅、正厅、内厅和后罩楼。正厅与内厅之间是一座南北狭长的庭院，两侧叠置假山，峰峦叠嶂，古树掩映，充满野趣。吴宅今为苏州工艺美术博物馆，展出瑞光塔真珠舍利宝幢（精仿）和近千件近现代苏州工艺精品。

· · · · ·
English

The Wu Residence was built during the Qianlong reign of the Qing.During the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom period, it was requisitioned by Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King, to house his family.

The residence includes east, middle, and west roads; the middle road is the most imposing, with a gate hall, main hall, inner hall, and rear covering hall from south to north.

Between the main hall and inner hall is a long north-south courtyard, with rockeries piled on both sides, overlapping peaks, and ancient trees shading the area—full of wild charm.

The Wu Residence is now the Suzhou Arts and Crafts Museum, exhibiting a fine replica of the Pearl Relic Stupa from Ruiguang Pagoda and nearly a thousand modern and contemporary Suzhou craft masterpieces.

06 报恩寺
Baoen Temple
宋—清
级别 Level
第六批全国重点文物保护单位（2006年）

姑苏区人民路1918号
类型 Type
佛寺/古塔
门票 Ticket
25元

中文原文

报恩寺始建于三国赤乌年间（238—251），是孙权为乳母陈氏所建，时称通玄寺。唐初改称开元寺，五代末年始称报恩寺。南宋绍兴二十二年（1152年）寺人募建报恩寺塔，俗称北寺塔。

今寺庙包括宋代的报恩寺塔、明代的石柱牌坊和不染尘观音殿、清代的古铜佛殿和藏经阁等。

寺前牌坊建于明万历四十五年（1617年），原在马医科巷申时行祠前，1979年移至此地。这是一座四柱三间五楼牌坊，有三重檐屋顶。

下部立四根石柱，其上木构部分皆用香樟木和楠木，屋顶脊端饰以开口哺龙和铁绣花，戗角上塑松鹤、雄狮和飞龙等。牌坊比例匀称，雕刻精美，为明代精品。报恩寺塔建于南宋，2006年列为第六批国保单位。

这是一座八角九层砖塔，外观挺拔高耸，是苏州城的标志建筑。其中六层以下为南宋遗构，六层以上推测为明代重建，内外木构件在清代更换过。塔平面为两圈砖筒体内外相套，外部各层皆有平座腰檐，仿木塔式样。

塔内设木梯，可层层登临，俯瞰苏州城。塔底部须弥座上的雕刻，塔内以砖仿木构的梁枋、斗栱和藻井，以及第三层塔心室的过道顶部用砖砌的小斗八藻井，都体现了宋代建筑的特征。

观音殿始建于南宋绍兴年间，明万历二十八年（1600年）重建，清代重修。大殿采用重檐歇山顶，外部立抹角方石檐柱，内柱则用楠木。

古铜佛殿建于清康熙十年（1671年），清光绪三十三年（1907年）重修，是一座七开间殿宇。

此外寺内还有《张士诚纪功碑》，1982年列为省保单位，描绘元至正十九年（1359年）张士诚在隆平府（苏州）宴请元朝使臣伯颜的场景，有118名浮雕人物。

· · · · ·
English

Baoen Temple was founded during the Chiwu reign of the Three Kingdoms (238-251), built by Sun Quan for his wet nurse Lady Chen, then called Tongxuan Temple.

In the early Tang it was renamed Kaiyuan Temple; at the end of the Five Dynasties it began to be called Baoen Temple.

In the 22nd year of Shaoxing of the Southern Song (1152), temple members raised funds to build the Baoen Temple Pagoda, commonly called the North Temple Pagoda.

Today the temple includes the Song-dynasty Baoen Temple Pagoda, the Ming-dynasty stone-pillar memorial archway and Buaran Chen Guanyin Hall, and the Qing-dynasty Ancient Bronze Buddha Hall and Scripture Depository.

The memorial archway in front of the temple was built in the 45th year of Wanli of the Ming (1617), originally in front of the Shen Shixing Shrine in Mayike Lane, moved here in 1979.

It is a four-pillar, three-bay, five-roof archway with triple-eave roofs.

Four stone pillars stand at the bottom; the wooden parts above are all made of camphor and nanmu wood, with open-mouthed dragons and iron flowers at the ridge ends, and molded pine cranes, lions, and flying dragons on the upturned corners.

The archway is well-proportioned with exquisite carvings—a Ming-dynasty masterpiece.

The Baoen Temple Pagoda was built in the Southern Song and designated a 6th-batch national protected site in 2006.

It is an octagonal nine-story brick pagoda, tall and straight in appearance, a landmark of Suzhou.

The lower six stories are Southern Song original; the upper six are presumed to have been rebuilt in the Ming, with internal and external wooden components replaced in the Qing.

The pagoda's plan consists of two nested brick cylinders; each external story has a flat balcony and waist eave, imitating a wooden pagoda style.

A wooden staircase inside allows climbing story by story for a bird's-eye view of Suzhou.

The carvings on the Sumeru pedestal at the pagoda's base, the brick-imitation wooden beams, brackets, and caisson ceilings inside, and the small douba caisson ceiling of brick at the corridor top of the third-story chamber all reflect Song-dynasty architectural features.

The Guanyin Hall was first built in the Shaoxing reign of the Southern Song, rebuilt in the 28th year of Wanli of the Ming (1600), and repaired in the Qing.

The main hall has a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, with chamfered square stone eave columns outside and nanmu columns inside.

The Ancient Bronze Buddha Hall was built in the 10th year of Kangxi of the Qing (1671) and repaired in the 33rd year of Guangxu (1907), a seven-bay hall.

Additionally, the temple contains the "Zhang Shicheng Merit Stele," designated a provincial protected site in 1982, depicting the scene in the 19th year of Zhizheng of the Yuan (1359) of Zhang Shicheng entertaining the Yuan envoy Boyan at Longping Prefecture (Suzhou), with 118 relief figures.

07 五峰园
Wufeng Garden
明
级别 Level
第五批江苏省保（2002年）
地址 Address
阊门西街47号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
2元
开放时间 Hours
9:00-18:00
中文原文

五峰园为明南京尚书杨成（字汝大）的别业，据传为文徵明之侄文伯仁设计，园中最重要的是南部山上的五块湖石，传为北宋朱勔"花石纲"遗物。今仅存一进庭院，布局洗练，体现了明代的园林风格。

园门朝西，入门是座小门厅，西侧开圆窗，从中可窥见亭榭山石，向左沿曲廊步入园中。园林主体是一厅、一池和一山。主厅五峰山房位于北侧，紧贴园墙坐北朝南，三开间加上周围廊共五间，与南面的五峰对应。厅南有一小片平地，前有水池与假山相依相绕，池中设汀步通向假山。

假山被水池划分成两处，东侧主山用湖石堆叠，不见泥土，下有石洞可穿行，上立丈人、观音、三老、庆云和擎天五峰，象征庐山五老峰。五块湖石皱透有致，为石中上品，这种并置的方式体现了明代中期的赏石品位。西侧辅山为土山，低矮平缓，作为主山的陪衬，山上建六角柳毅亭，纪念说书艺人柳毅。

亭子北侧是旱船柱石舫，有前舱、中舱和后舱，逐级增高，仿佛向南行驶。

· · · · ·
English

Wufeng Garden was the villa of Yang Cheng (style name Ruda), a Ming-dynasty Nanjing Minister, reportedly designed by Wen Boren, nephew of Wen Zhengming.

The most important feature is the five Taihu rocks on the southern hill, said to be relics of the "Flower and Stone Convoy" of Zhu Mian in the Northern Song.

Today only one courtyard remains, with a concise layout reflecting Ming-dynasty garden style.

The garden gate faces west; entering is a small gate hall, with a round window on the west side through which pavilions and rocks can be glimpsed; turning left along a winding corridor leads into the garden.

The garden's main body is one hall, one pond, and one hill.

The main hall Wufeng Shanfang (Five Peak Mountain Room) is on the north side, against the garden wall facing south—three bays plus surrounding corridors totaling five bays, corresponding to the five peaks to the south.

South of the hall is a small flat area, with a pond and rockery intertwined; stepping stones in the pond lead to the rockery.

The rockery is divided by the pond into two parts: the eastern main hill is piled with Taihu rocks with no visible soil, with a stone cave below to pass through, and five peaks above—Zhangren (Elder), Guanyin, Sanlao (Three Elders), Qingyun (Auspicious Cloud), and Qingtian (Supporting the Sky)—symbolizing the Five Old Men Peaks of Mount Lu.

The five Taihu rocks are wrinkled and perforated, top-grade stones; this arrangement reflects the rock-appreciation taste of the mid-Ming.

The western secondary hill is an earth hill, low and gentle, serving as a foil to the main hill, with a hexagonal Liuyi Pavilion on top commemorating the storyteller Liu Yi.

North of the pavilion is the land-boat Zhushi Fang (Pillar Stone Boat), with front, middle, and rear cabins rising step by step, as if sailing south.

建筑要点 / Key Features
明南京尚书杨成别业；文徵明之侄文伯仁设计；五块湖石（花石纲遗物）；丈人观音三老庆云擎天五峰；旱船柱石舫
08 艺圃
Yipu Garden
明—清
级别 Level
世界文化遗产，第六批全国重点文物保护单位（2006年）
地址 Address
姑苏区文衙弄5号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
10元
开放时间 Hours
7:30-17:00（16:30停止售票）
中文原文

艺圃前身是明嘉靖三十八年（1559年）袁祖庚（1519—1590）建造的醉颖堂。万历末年归文震孟（1574—1636），拓建后更名药圃，大致奠定今日格局。

清顺治十七年（1660年）归山东莱阳人姜埰（1607—1673），更名敬亭山房，成为当时明遗民的重要活动场所，有众多园记和园图传世，如姜埰作《颐圃记》《疏柳亭记》，汪琬作《姜氏艺圃记》《艺圃后记》，王翚绘《艺圃图》。后来其子姜实节更名艺圃。

清康熙三十五年（1696年）园归商人吴斌，清道光三年（1823年）归吴传熊，清道光十九年（1839年）又归绸业公所，改名七襄公所。

新中国成立后曾租作民居、校舍和工厂等，20世纪80年代修复开放，2000年作为苏州古典园林扩展项目，列入世界文化遗产名录。艺圃采取东宅西园的格局，东、北以建筑为主，西、南以山池为主。入口在东南角，穿过小院、游廊到达朝西的思嗜轩。轩北为东路建筑，自南向北依次为爱莲窝、世纶堂（姜埰时期名延光阁）和东莱草堂。

堂东为饽饪斋小院，曾是姜埰书房。中路北端为博雅堂，前身是文震孟世纶堂，姜埰重建为念祖堂，当时作为园中主堂，前有开阔的庭院，可隔池欣赏南岸假山；七襄公所时期在庭院临池处建水榭，堂前仅留下一处天井小院，内叠湖石花台，其主堂地位被水榭取代。水榭今名延光阁，阁东旸谷书堂是姜实节读书讲学处，堂西敬亭山房原为文震孟的青瑶屿。

沿池西的响月廊可去往水池南岸，游廊中段扩大为半亭，可隔池赏月。池东南和西南各有一座石桥，掩住水尾，悠远不尽。池南以大假山为主体，堆土而成，外叠黄石和湖石，文震孟在山上置高二丈的五老峰，姜埰又在山顶筑朝爽台，置垂云峰，作为池北主堂的对景。

后来假山被毁，20世纪80年代依附土山用湖石重叠，北面临池叠成峭壁，用湖石砌驳岸、石矶，山内藏石洞，山间有石道可登山顶朝爽亭。七襄公所时期在假山西南角围成浴鸥小院，院内叠假山一角，并从三折渡香桥和粉墙下引入池水，构成一处精致的园中园。

园北、园东各有一门，分别通向外部假山的前部和后部。由池南假山东北角石桥可去往东岸乳鱼亭，姜埰时建，保留了明代风格，是欣赏池北厅堂和池南山林的佳处。艺圃主体为一堂一池一山，布局简练疏朗，水池东、北、西三岸较为平直，保持了明代园林的格调。

乳鱼亭和博雅堂皆为清初重建的明式建筑。西南角的园中园虽为后期所筑，但手法精妙，自成幽境。

· · · · ·
English

The predecessor of Yipu Garden was the Zuiying Hall built by Yuan Zugeng (1519-1590) in the 38th year of Jiajing of the Ming (1559).

In the late Wanli period it passed to Wen Zhenmeng (1574-1636), who expanded and renamed it Yaopu (Herb Garden), roughly establishing today's layout.

In the 17th year of Shunzhi of the Qing (1660), it passed to Jiang Cai (1607-1673) of Laiyang, Shandong, who renamed it Jingting Shanfang (Jingting Mountain Room), becoming an important gathering place for Ming loyalists at the time, with numerous garden records and paintings surviving—such as Jiang Cai's "Yipu Record" and "Sparse Willow Pavilion Record," Wang Wan's "Jiang Family Yipu Record" and "Postscript to Yipu Record," and Wang Hui's "Painting of Yipu.

" Later his son Jiang Shijie renamed it Yipu.

In the 35th year of Kangxi (1696) the garden passed to merchant Wu Bin; in the 3rd year of Daoguang (1823) to Wu Chuanxiong; in the 19th year of Daoguang (1839) to the Silk Guild, renamed Qixiang Gongsuo.

After the founding of New China, it was rented as residences, schools, and factories; restored and opened in the 1980s; in 2000, as an extension of Suzhou Classical Gardens, it was inscribed on the World Cultural Heritage List.

Yipu adopts an east-residence, west-garden layout, with buildings dominating the east and north, and hills and ponds dominating the west and south.

The entrance is at the southeast corner; passing through a small courtyard and corridor reaches the west-facing Sishi Xuan.

North of the studio are east-road buildings, from south to north: Ailian Wo (Lotus-Loving Nest), Shilun Tang (Jiang Cai period name Yanguang Ge), and Donglai Caotang (East Lai Thatched Hall).

East of the hall is the Boren Zhai small courtyard, once Jiang Cai's study.

At the north end of the middle road is Boya Tang (Elegant Hall), formerly Wen Zhenmeng's Shilun Tang; Jiang Cai rebuilt it as Nianzu Tang, then the garden's main hall with an open courtyard in front for admiring the south-bank rockery across the pond; during the Qixiang Gongsuo period, a waterside pavilion was built at the pond side of the courtyard, leaving only a small courtyard in front of the hall with a Taihu rock flower terrace—its status as main hall was replaced by the waterside pavilion.

The waterside pavilion is now called Yanguang Ge (Extended Light Pavilion); east of it, Yanggu Shutang was Jiang Shijie's study and lecture place; west of it, Jingting Shanfang was originally Wen Zhenmeng's Qingyao Yu.

Along the Xiangyue Corridor west of the pond, one can reach the south bank of the pond; the middle section of the corridor expands into a half-pavilion for moon-viewing across the pond.

There are stone bridges at the southeast and southwest of the pond, concealing the water's tail for a sense of endless distance.

South of the pond, a large rockery forms the main body—piled with earth and faced with yellow stone and Taihu rocks.

Wen Zhenmeng placed the five-old-peak, two-zhang high on the hill; Jiang Cai built the Zhaoshuang Terrace at the top with the Chuiyun Peak, serving as the opposite scene for the main hall north of the pond.

The rockery was later destroyed; in the 1980s it was rebuilt with Taihu rocks against the earth hill, with cliffs facing the pond, Taihu rock retaining walls and stone banks, a stone cave hidden inside, and a stone path up to the Zhaoshuang Pavilion at the top.

During the Qixiang Gongsuo period, the Yu'ou (Gull Bathing) small courtyard was enclosed at the southwest corner of the rockery, with a corner of rockery inside and pond water introduced through the three-fold Duxiang Bridge and under the white wall—forming an exquisite garden-within-a-garden.

There are gates at the north and east of the garden, leading to the front and rear of the external rockery respectively.

From the stone bridge at the northeast corner of the south-bank rockery, one can reach the east-bank Ruyu Pavilion (Milk Fish Pavilion), built in Jiang Cai's time, retaining Ming style—a fine place for admiring the north-bank halls and south-bank mountain forest.

Yipu's main body is one hall, one pond, and one hill, with a concise and open layout; the east, north, and west banks of the pond are relatively straight, maintaining the Ming-dynasty garden style.

Both the Ruyu Pavilion and Boya Tang are early-Qing reconstructions in Ming style.

The garden-within-a-garden at the southwest corner, though built later, is exquisitely crafted, forming its own secluded realm.

09 环秀山庄
Huanxiu Manor
明—清
级别 Level
世界文化遗产，第三批全国重点文物保护单位（1988年）
地址 Address
姑苏区景德路272号
类型 Type
古典园林
门票 Ticket
15元
开放时间 Hours
8:30-16:30（16:00停止售票）
中文原文

环秀山庄的主体建于清中期，但五代时期这里就有广陵王钱氏的金谷园，宋代为朱文长乐圃，元明时期先后为景德寺、学道书院和兵巡道衙门等。

明万历年间首辅申时行告老还乡后在此建赐闲堂宅园，其后代改筑为蘧园。清乾隆初年园归刑部员外郎蒋楫，叠山凿池，形成今日园林雏形，园中"飞雪"泉便为当时所凿，其后又归尚书毕沅。

清嘉庆十二年（1807年）大学士孙士毅之孙孙均聘请戈裕良重构此园，叠筑园北主体假山，使其成为一代名园。

清道光二十九年（1849年）汪藻、汪坤在园旁建宗祠、义庄，围绕假山建问泉亭、补秋舫，并将山南主堂命名为环秀山庄，形成今日格局。太平天国时期园林有所毁伤，"文革"期间在园内建厂房，砍伐古木，破坏最严重。所幸山体保存良好，"文革"后予以精心修复。

1988年列为全国重点文物保护单位，1997年底列入世界文化遗产名录。今园林入口在东侧，东墙外有海棠亭，从西百花巷程宅移来，传为康熙朝香山艺人徐振明所建，平面、宝顶、装饰皆以海棠为主题，形式别致。

入门向北为前宅部分，包括有谷堂和环秀山庄主厅共两进，屋前皆有小院，一方一扁，点缀木石。主厅为鸳鸯厅，采用欲扬先抑手法，南侧庭院狭小，穿过主堂，北院豁然开朗。宽敞的平台北部矗立一座湖石假山，周围流水环绕，亭廊相依，是全园最精华的部分，面积虽小却足以使环秀山庄跻身名园之列。

这座假山占满了北园全区，非但不显拥塞，反觉气势雄浑，水池、轩房、廊亭皆为配合假山而设。其中西南为假山主峰，山脉自东向西奔注，气势连绵，于西侧池边戛然而止，形成悬崖峭壁之势，并在西南角突起一峰作为高潮。山间斜引入一道溪流，蜿蜒屈曲，溪北山间筑石室，西南则藏幽深岩穴，人行涧底如游深山。

溪流东南顶部架设平桥，构成立体交通，游人可出溪循西南石道登山，周览园景，俯瞰涧谷。由山顶可至假山东北，此处为缓坡土丘，多植花木，与前山的峻嶒峻峭形成对比。山顶建"半潭秋水一房山"方亭，其东有爬山廊通向补秋山房，皆为静坐赏山之所。由房北廊路向西通往西北次山，此山宛如西南主山的余脉，与主山隔问泉亭遥相呼应。

山岩虽小，却崖涧洞壑兼具，自成一体，石壁上题"飞雪"二字，为古泉遗迹。问泉亭处在两山之间，位置极佳，可近赏南山，北望石壁，仰听飞泉，俯观清池。由问泉亭向南折入东侧游廊，向西通向景德路274号的王鏊祠，1995年列为省保单位。

王鏊（1449—1534）明正德年间官至少傅、户部尚书、武英殿大学士，后来退居苏州整理地方文献，纂有《姑苏志》和《震泽编》等。明嘉靖十一年（1532年）其子王延哲奏请朝廷在景德寺废址为他建祠堂，今存头门、过厅和享堂共三进，现为中国苏绣艺术博物馆，与环秀山庄联合开放（梅雨季节会关闭）。

· · · · ·
English

The main body of Huanxiu Manor was built in the mid-Qing, but as early as the Five Dynasties this site had the Jingu Garden of the Guangling King Qian family; in the Song it was Zhu Wen's Changle Garden; in the Yuan and Ming it successively served as Jingde Temple, Xuedao Academy, and the military circuit intendant's yamen.

During the Wanli reign of the Ming, Grand Secretary Shen Shixing, after retiring to his hometown, built the Cixian Hall residence garden here; his descendants rebuilt it as Qu Garden.

In the early Qianlong of the Qing, the garden passed to Jiang Ji, a vice director of the Ministry of Justice, who piled rockeries and dug ponds, forming the prototype of today's garden—the "Feixue" (Flying Snow) spring was dug at this time.

It later passed to Minister Bi Yuan.

In the 12th year of Jiaqing (1807), Sun Jun, grandson of Grand Secretary Sun Shiyi, hired Ge Yuliang to reconstruct the garden, piling the main rockery north of the garden and making it a famous garden of the era.

In the 29th year of Daoguang (1849), Wang Zao and Wang Kun built an ancestral hall and charity estate beside the garden, constructing the Wenquan Pavilion and Buqiu Fang around the rockery, and naming the south main hall Huanxiu Shanzhuang (Embracing Beauty Mountain Villa)—forming today's layout.

During the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom period the garden suffered damage; during the Cultural Revolution, factory buildings were erected inside and ancient trees felled—the most severe destruction.

Fortunately the mountain body was well preserved and carefully restored after the Cultural Revolution.

Designated a National Key Cultural Heritage Site in 1988 and inscribed on the World Cultural Heritage List at the end of 1997.

Today the garden entrance is on the east side; outside the east wall is the Haitang (Crabapple) Pavilion, moved from the Cheng residence at West Baihua Lane, said to be built by Xu Zhenming, a Xiangshan artisan of the Kangxi court, with plan, finial, and decoration all themed on crabapples—unusual in form.

Entering northward is the front residence section, including the Yougu Hall and the main hall Huanxiu Shanzhuang—two bays total, each with a small courtyard in front, one square and one oblong, dotted with trees and rocks.

The main hall is a mandarin-duck hall, using the "suppress before elevating" technique: the south courtyard is narrow; passing through the main hall, the north courtyard suddenly opens up.

North of the spacious platform stands a Taihu rockery, surrounded by flowing water with pavilions and corridors—the essence of the whole garden.

Though small in area, it is enough to place Huanxiu Manor among famous gardens.

This rockery fills the entire northern garden, not feeling cramped but rather imposing; the pond, studios, and corridors are all designed to complement the rockery.

The southwest is the main peak, with the mountain range rushing from east to west in continuous momentum, stopping abruptly at the west pond edge to form cliff faces, with a peak rising at the southwest corner as the climax.

A stream winds diagonally into the mountain; north of the stream a stone chamber is built, while deep rock caves are hidden to the southwest—walking along the stream bed feels like wandering in deep mountains.

A flat bridge spans the top of the stream's southeast end, creating three-dimensional circulation; visitors can exit the stream and climb the mountain via the southwest stone path, surveying the garden and overlooking the ravine.

From the mountaintop one can reach the northeast of the rockery, a gentle earth slope planted with flowers and trees, contrasting with the jagged steepness of the front mountain.

On the mountaintop stands the square pavilion "Bantan Qiushui Yi Fangshan" (Half Pool Autumn Water, One Room Mountain); to its east a climbing corridor leads to the Buqiu Shanfang (Autumn-Complementing Mountain Room), both places for sitting quietly and admiring the mountain.

From the corridor north of the room, a path leads west to the northwest secondary hill, like an offshoot of the southwest main peak, echoing the main mountain across the Wenquan Pavilion.

Though small, the rock has cliffs, ravines, caves, and gullies, self-contained; the stone wall is inscribed with "Feixue" (Flying Snow), a relic of the ancient spring.

The Wenquan Pavilion sits between the two mountains, excellently positioned for close admiration of the south mountain, northward view of the stone wall, upward listening to the flying spring, and downward gazing at the clear pond.

From Wenquan Pavilion, turning south into the east corridor leads west to the Wang Ao Ancestral Hall at No.274 Jingde Road, designated a provincial protected site in 1995.

Wang Ao (1449-1534) served as Junior Tutor, Minister of Revenue, and Grand Secretary of the Wuying Hall in the Zhengde reign of the Ming, later retiring to Suzhou to organize local documents, compiling the "Gusu Gazetteer" and "Zhenze Compilation.

" In the 11th year of Jiajing of the Ming (1532), his son Wang Yanzhe petitioned the court to build a shrine for him on the former Jingde Temple site.

Today three bays survive: gate hall, passage hall, and offering hall—now the Chinese Suzhou Embroidery Art Museum, jointly open with Huanxiu Manor (closed during plum rain season).

10 城隍庙
Temple of City God
明—清
级别 Level
第二批江苏省保（1982年）
地址 Address
姑苏区景德路94号
类型 Type
祠庙
门票 Ticket
免费开放
开放时间 Hours
8:00-16:30
中文原文

苏州早在宋元时期就建有城隍庙，当时位于子城西南角，元末毁于兵火。明洪武三年（1370年）在今址重建，其后多次重修。各地城隍大多由有功于当地民众的英雄、名臣担任，各不相同，苏州的城隍老爷是战国四公子之一的黄歇。

今苏州城隍庙尚存头门、仪门、大殿和寝殿。仪门为清同治十二年（1873年）重建，其北大殿平面呈工字形，前后两殿以穿堂相连，俗称工字殿，是苏州唯一保存完整的明初建筑。

工字殿前殿宽五间，单檐歇山顶，内部正中供城隍，两侧立赏善、罚恶两司；后殿比前殿略小，供月下老人、城隍娘娘和几尊土地神。殿内最珍贵的是嵌在后殿西次间前檐墙上的《三横四直图》碑。

此碑立于清嘉庆二年（1797年），记载嘉庆初年吴中官绅商民募款疏浚城内河道的始末。碑的背面绘刻苏城河道图，以"三横四直"七条贯穿全城的干流为主河道，并标有城垣及重要桥梁、寺观和衙署的位置，形象地展示了清中期苏州的水城风貌。

· · · · ·
English

Suzhou had a City God Temple as early as the Song and Yuan dynasties, then located at the southwest corner of the Zicheng (sub-city), destroyed by war at the end of the Yuan.

In the 3rd year of Hongwu of the Ming (1370), it was rebuilt at the present site and subsequently repaired multiple times.

City gods in different places are usually local heroes or famous officials who served the people—varying by place; Suzhou's City God is Huang Xie, one of the Four Princes of the Warring States.

Today Suzhou's City God Temple retains the gate hall, ceremonial gate, main hall, and bedchamber hall.The ceremonial gate was rebuilt in the 12th year of Tongzhi of the Qing (1873).

The main hall to its north has a gong (I)-shaped plan, with front and rear halls connected by a covered corridor—commonly called the Gongzi Hall (I-shaped Hall), the only completely surviving early-Ming building in Suzhou.

The front hall of the I-shaped hall is five bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; inside, the City God is enshrined in the center, with the Reward-Good and Punish-Evil departments on both sides.

The rear hall is slightly smaller than the front, enshrining the Old Man Under the Moon, the City God's Lady, and several Earth Gods.

The most precious item in the hall is the "Three Horizontal Four Vertical Map" stele embedded in the front eave wall of the west secondary bay of the rear hall.

Erected in the 2nd year of Jiaqing of the Qing (1797), it records the始末 of officials, gentry, merchants, and residents of Wu raising funds to dredge the city's waterways in the early Jiaqing period.

The back of the stele is engraved with a map of Suzhou's waterways, using the "three horizontal, four vertical" seven main waterways贯穿 the whole city as the main channels, and marking the positions of city walls, important bridges, temples, and yamen—vividly showing the water-city appearance of mid-Qing Suzhou.

11 俞樾故居（曲园）
Former Residence of Yu Yue (Quyuan Garden)
清
级别 Level
第六批全国重点文物保护单位（2006年）
地址 Address
姑苏区人民路马医科巷43号
类型 Type
故居/园林
门票 Ticket
免费
开放时间 Hours
8:00-11:00, 11:45-16:00
中文原文

俞樾（1821—1907）字荫甫，号曲园居士，浙江德清人，清末著名学者。

清同治十三年（1874年）俞樾在苏州旧城马医科巷购得潘世恩废宅，改建为侍母之所；并与夫人在宅西、北隙地上筑园，因平面形似曲尺，故取《老子》"曲则全"之意，命名为曲园，俞樾自号"曲园居士"，作《曲园记》。

清光绪五年（1879年）俞樾在春在堂南添建小竹里馆及其前庭院，清光绪十八年（1892年）又整修曲水池桥亭。这处故居采用东宅西园格局。

东路前部为外堂，包括门厅、轿厅和正厅乐知堂共三进，皆为三间；后部为两进五间内宅，构成倒凸字形的吉宅平面。由轿厅前院向西可进入小竹里馆前院，"文革"期间被毁，已非原貌。小竹里馆北为春在堂，取"花落春仍在"之意，1850年俞樾中进士时因此句获得曾国藩赏识，晚年又将著述编为《春在堂全书》。

堂北庭园是全园精华所在。居中为池，曲水亭、达斋、艮宦紧贴西墙、北墙布置，并以长廊相连，假山则贴东墙堆筑，与亭廊隔池相对。俞樾《曲园记》称："所谓达斋者，与春轩南北相值。所谓曲水亭者，与回峰阁东西相值。艮宦则最居东北隅，故以艮名。艮，止也。园止此也。然艮宦南有小门，自吾内室往，可从此入，则又首艮宦。艮固成终成始也。"这段话总结了曲园的造园意匠。

庭园以方形的曲水池为中心，采用轴线对称布置：西岸居中的曲水亭与东岸假山上的回峰阁正对，园北的达斋与园南的春在轩正对，艮宦则因位于东北角而得名，有终止之意，但俞樾经常从这里入园，又具起始之意，从而使这座小园有始有终，首尾相接。曲园对称严整的布局在苏州园林中非常罕见，颇得中国早期园林简洁方正的意趣。

· · · · ·
English

Yu Yue (1821-1907), style name Yinfu, hao Quyuan Jushi (Quyuan Dweller), was a native of Deqing, Zhejiang, and a famous scholar of the late Qing.

In the 13th year of Tongzhi of the Qing (1874), Yu Yue purchased the abandoned residence of Pan Shien in Mayike Lane in the old city of Suzhou, converting it into a residence for serving his mother; and with his wife, built a garden on the vacant land west and north of the residence.

Because its plan resembled a carpenter's square (quchi), he took the meaning of "the crooked becomes whole" from the Laozi, naming it Quyuan (Crooked Garden).

Yu Yue called himself "Quyuan Jushi" and wrote the "Record of Quyuan.

" In the 5th year of Guangxu (1879), Yu Yue added the Xiaozhuli Guan (Small Bamboo Grove Studio) and its front courtyard south of the Chunzai Tang; in the 18th year of Guangxu (1892) he renovated the Qushui Pond bridge and pavilions.

This former residence adopts an east-residence, west-garden layout.

The front of the east road is the outer hall, including gate hall, sedan hall, and main hall Lezhi Tang—three bays each, three bays total.

The rear is two bays of five-bay inner residence, forming an inverted-convex auspicious residence plan.

From the sedan hall's front courtyard, turning west leads to the Xiaozhuli Guan front courtyard—destroyed during the Cultural Revolution, no longer original.

North of Xiaozhuli Guan is Chunzai Tang (Spring Remains Hall), taking the meaning "flowers fall but spring remains"; in 1850, when Yu Yue passed the jinshi examination, this phrase won Zeng Guofan's appreciation, and in his later years he compiled his writings as the "Complete Works of Chunzai Tang.

" The garden north of the hall is the essence of the whole garden.

A pond occupies the center; the Qushui Ting (Winding Water Pavilion), Dazhai, and Genhuan are arranged against the west and north walls, connected by a long corridor, while a rockery is piled against the east wall, facing the pavilions and corridor across the pond.

Yu Yue's "Record of Quyuan" states: "The so-called Dazhai faces the Chunxuan north-south.The so-called Qushui Ting faces the Huifeng Pavilion east-west.

Genhuan is at the northeast corner, hence named Gen.Gen means stopping.The garden ends here.

Yet south of Genhuan there is a small gate; from my inner chamber one can enter here, then Genhuan is again the beginning.Gen indeed completes both end and beginning.

" This passage summarizes Quyuan's garden design intent.

The courtyard centers on the square Qushui Pond, adopting axis-symmetrical layout: the Qushui Ting in the center of the west bank faces the Huifeng Pavilion on the east-bank rockery; the Dazhai north of the garden faces the Chunzai Xuan south of the garden; Genhuan is named for its northeast corner position, meaning termination, but Yu Yue often entered the garden from here, giving it the meaning of beginning—thus this small garden has both beginning and end, connected head to tail.

Quyuan's symmetrical and rigorous layout is very rare among Suzhou gardens, capturing the simplicity and rectitude of early Chinese gardens.

Heyuan Garden

中文原文

鹤园位于姑苏区韩家巷4号，2011年列为省保单位，今为政协办公地，不开放。据金天羽《鹤园记》记载，清光绪三十三年（1907年）洪鹭汀在宅西筑园，俞樾为题"携鹤草堂"匾，因名鹤园。园林尚未完工便卖给庞庆麟（字小雅，号屈庐），后归其孙庞国钧（字蘅裳），1923年重修。

园南有五间门厅，其西墙上开漏窗可窥见园景。入门后以长廊串起四面厅、风亭、书房、携鹤草堂和月亭等建筑，围绕着中央的曲池，沿庭院周边布置山石和花木等。园林东面是长廊，自南而北贯通全园，连接门厅、四面厅、风亭与主厅。长廊与墙壁间形成多处隙地，其中栽花种竹，与水池主院构成对比。池边叠砌湖石，配植丁香、海棠等花木，西南角延伸出水湾，上架石桥。水湾指向庭园西南角的土山，上建六角亭并植藤萝灌木，颇具山林气息。

· · · · ·
English

Heyuan Garden is located at No.4 Hanjia Lane, Gusu District, designated a provincial protected site in 2011, now used as CPPCC offices and not open to the public.

According to Jin Tianyu's "Record of Heyuan," in the 33rd year of Guangxu of the Qing (1907), Hong Luting built a garden west of his residence; Yu Yue inscribed the plaque "Xiehe Caotang" (Carrying Crane Thatched Hall), hence the name Heyuan (Crane Garden).

Before the garden was completed, it was sold to Pang Qinglin (style name Xiaoya, hao Qulu), later passing to his grandson Pang Guojun (style name Hengshang), who rebuilt it in 1923.

South of the garden is a five-bay gate hall, with lattice windows on its west wall offering glimpses of the garden scenery.

Entering, a long corridor connects the Simian Hall (Four-Sided Hall), Feng Ting (Wind Pavilion), study, Xiehe Caotang, and Yue Ting (Moon Pavilion), surrounding the central curved pond, with rocks, trees, and flowers arranged along the courtyard perimeter.

The east side of the garden is a long corridor running from south to north through the entire garden, connecting the gate hall, Simian Hall, Feng Ting, and main hall.

Between the corridor and walls are multiple open spaces planted with flowers and bamboo, contrasting with the main pond courtyard.

Taihu rocks are piled by the pond, planted with lilac, crabapple, and other flowers and trees; a water inlet extends from the southwest corner, spanned by a stone bridge.

The water inlet points to an earth hill at the southwest corner of the courtyard, topped with a hexagonal pavilion and planted with wisteria and shrubs—quite a mountain-forest atmosphere.

13 吴云宅园（听枫园）
Residence and Garden of Wu Yun (Tingfeng Garden)
